pedagogy.summary: Simple chance experiments are the child's hands-on entry to probability: flip a coin, roll a die, or draw counters many times, record each trial in a tally chart, and compare what happened with what was expected. The procedural goal is disciplined trial-by-trial recording and a sensible read of the results — seeing that outcomes cluster near the expected split without matching it exactly, and that each trial is independent of the last.
bestPractices: Have children predict the expected outcome first ('about half heads'), then run and record, so the comparison is theirs to make
Enforce one-tally-per-trial recording as the trial happens, not reconstruction from memory, and total the marks against the number of trials
Pool results across the class to show a larger sample landing closer to the expected split than any one child's 20 trials
Explicitly discuss why 13 heads out of 20 does NOT mean the coin is broken — short runs vary
Confront 'it's due' / 'heads again' talk on the spot: the coin has no memory, each flip is independent
keyRepresentations: Tally chart / frequency table (one row per outcome)
Coins, dice, and bags of counters as trial-generators
Bar or block chart of observed frequencies against the expected line
commonMisconceptions: Expecting the experiment to match the theoretical split exactly, and concluding the device is biased when it does not (law of small numbers)
Recency thinking — predicting the next trial from the recent run ('it's been heads four times, so tails is due', or 'heads is on a streak')
Recording carelessly — backfilling tallies or losing count so the total does not match the number of trials
Treating the result of a small experiment as the true probability rather than an estimate

learn.summary: Children aged 9–10 learn probability through hands-on chance experiments: predict an expected outcome, flip a coin / roll a die / draw counters many times, record each trial one-tally-at-a-time in a tally chart, and compare what happened with what was expected. Core insights: a fair device produces outcomes that cluster near but rarely exactly match the expected split, so expecting an exact match and concluding the device is biased from too few trials is the law-of-small-numbers error; each trial is independent of the last (no 'it's due' recency thinking); and a small experiment estimates rather than proves the true probability. With a fair device, running or pooling many more trials usually brings the observed proportion closer to the expected split, though not to an exact match.

activities.title: Predict, flip, tally: run and read a coin experiment
feedback: If a child gets 13 heads and 7 tails and says the coin is rigged or that they 'did it wrong', don't reteach the mechanics — explain that 20 trials is too few to judge fairness and short runs vary. Pool their flips with classmates' to reach 100+ and see whether the proportion moves nearer to half (with a fair coin it usually does, though not exactly).

If the tally total doesn't equal 20, or marks were backfilled from memory, this is an execution lapse: support a one-mark-immediately-per-flip routine with a running count rather than reteaching the concept.
If the child did get close to half, affirm reading it as 'about half, but not exactly ten' — close to the expected split rather than an exact match.
activities.rationale: Conducting and recording is a procedure best learned by doing it, so the child owns the prediction-versus-result comparison. Predicting first makes the comparison theirs; one-tally-per-trial enforces disciplined recording; totalling against the trial count catches miscounts. Sources note that a small sample need not match the theoretical probability and that concluding bias from too few trials is a documented mistake.
sourceClaims: A small sample need not match the theoretical probability, and concluding bias from too few trials is a documented mistake: '20 times is not enough trials' — the more trials, the closer relative frequency gets to the theoretical probability.
learnerActions: Before flipping, predict the expected number of heads in 20 flips (about 10) and write it down.
Set up a tally chart with one row per outcome (heads, tails).
Flip the coin 20 times, marking exactly one tally per flip AS it happens — not reconstructing from memory afterward.
Total the marks and check the total equals the number of flips (20).
Describe what you notice: was it about half? Exactly ten? How close to your prediction?
activities.intendedInsight: A fair device produces outcomes clustered near the expected split but not exactly matching it; disciplined one-tally-per-trial recording is part of the procedure, and the total must reconcile with the number of trials.

activities.title: Watch the proportion settle: scale up the number of trials
feedback: If a child thinks 20 trials already proved the coin fair or unfair, draw attention to how much the proportion still wobbles at 20 versus how it usually steadies by a few hundred — the gap between the proportion of heads and one-half tends to narrow with more trials (even though the difference in raw counts of heads and tails can grow).
Name explicitly that the result of a small experiment is an estimate of the probability, not the true probability itself.
activities.rationale: Pooling to a larger sample and watching the proportion steady confronts the law of small numbers concretely — children typically see short-run variation give way to proportions close to (not exactly at) the expected split. A live tally with a running relative-frequency bar (that wobbles then steadies) and a 'run 20' versus 'run 500' contrast make this mechanism visible; manual single-trial mode preserves one-tally-per-trial experience before auto-running. These interaction examples are optional illustrations of the mechanism, not required tooling.
sourceClaims: A small sample need not match the theoretical probability, and concluding bias from too few trials is a documented mistake: '20 times is not enough trials' — the more trials, the closer relative frequency gets to the theoretical probability.
learnerActions: After a lopsided small sample (e.g. 13 heads in 20), keep going: pool results across the class, or keep flipping toward 100, 200, 500 trials.
Track both the growing tally AND the running proportion of heads as more trials accumulate.
Compare a 'small run' (20) against a 'large run' (hundreds): notice which lands closer to the expected half (usually, but not always, the large run).
State what the larger sample tells you that the small one couldn't.
activities.intendedInsight: For a fair coin, as the number of trials grows the observed proportion tends to move toward the expected split and steady; a lopsided 20-trial result can easily happen by chance with a fair coin, so on its own it is not evidence of bias. The small experiment gives an estimate, not the true probability.

activities.title: The coin has no memory: confront recency thinking
feedback: If the child predicts the next flip from the recent run ('it's been heads four times, tails is due') or seems surprised a streak 'kept going', state plainly that the coin has no memory and each flip is independent, then test it by predicting-then-flipping several times.
Reinforce: with a fair coin, a run of heads is just as likely to be followed by heads as by tails.
activities.rationale: Recency errors — both negative recency ('a tail is due') and positive recency (expecting a streak to continue) — reflect a failure to treat trials as independent and are documented across childhood. Predict-then-flip repetition surfaces the belief and tests it against outcomes so the child confronts it directly.
sourceClaims: Recency errors — both 'a tail is due' (negative recency, from the representativeness heuristic) and expecting a streak to continue (positive recency) — reflect a failure to treat successive trials as independent, and are documented across childhood.
learnerActions: After a run of several heads in a row, predict the next flip (or say it cannot be predicted) and say WHY.
Flip again and check; repeat the predict-then-flip several times.
Explain whether a streak of heads makes tails any more 'due' on the next flip.
State in your own words why each flip stays 50-50 regardless of what came before.
activities.intendedInsight: Successive trials are independent: the coin has no memory, so neither 'tails is due' (negative recency) nor 'heads is on a streak' (positive recency) is correct — each flip remains 50-50 whatever preceded it.

activities.title: Interpretation check: does a small sample prove bias?
feedback: If a child answers that 13–7 proves bias, point back to short-run variation and the need for more trials to judge fairness.

If a child says the next flip is 'due' to be tails (or that heads is 'hot'), restate that each flip is independent, so the streak does not change the odds; for a fair coin, heads and tails stay equally likely at 50-50.
activities.rationale: A recognition or multiple-choice format can test interpretation of a completed tally and reasoning about bias and independence, but it cannot deliver the hands-on conducting-and-recording practice; use it as a check alongside, not instead of, performing an experiment. This supports interpretation only — it does not elicit independent construction of the experiment.
sourceClaims: A small sample need not match the theoretical probability, and concluding bias from too few trials is a documented mistake: '20 times is not enough trials' — the more trials, the closer relative frequency gets to the theoretical probability.
learnerActions: Read a completed tally showing 13 heads and 7 tails out of 20 flips.
Decide whether this proves the coin is unfair, and explain your reasoning.
Say how you could check whether the coin is actually biased.
Given a streak of four heads, say whether the next flip is more likely to be heads, more likely tails, or neither — and explain why.
activities.intendedInsight: Judging fairness and independence from a completed record: 13 of 20 heads does not prove bias because 20 trials is too few; checking requires many more trials; and no run of heads changes the next flip's odds — for a fair coin, heads and tails remain equally likely.

constraints: The child must actually perform and tally the experiment; a recognition-only or reading-a-completed-tally task does not elicit the independent conducting-and-recording skill the topic requires.
Enforce one-tally-per-trial recording as the trial happens, not reconstruction from memory; total the marks against the number of trials so a mismatch is caught.
Have children predict the expected outcome before running, so the prediction-versus-result comparison is theirs to make.

Distinguish an execution lapse (careless recording, miscounting) from a conceptual error (expecting an exact match, recency thinking) — support the recording habit for the former, confront the belief for the latter.
A completed-tally interpretation check supports reasoning about bias and independence but is a supplement; it does not replace conducting the experiment.

Physical tossing (coin/die) and on-screen simulators offer different experiences — tactile realism versus the ability to scale rapidly to hundreds of trials; recording and comparing frequencies is not a spatial task, so neither is universally required. Treat the choice as a trade-off, not a ranking.
A small experiment yields an estimate of the probability, not the true probability; make this explicit to avoid treating a 20-trial result as definitive.
Live-tally, running proportion bar, 'run 20 vs run 500' contrast, and manual single-trial mode are optional illustrations of the mechanism, not mandatory tooling.
After any run, each flip of a fair coin stays 50-50 and heads is exactly as likely as tails next — never present one outcome as 'most likely' following a streak.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and the cited claims support teaching principles rather than proving any specific activity was tested.

Self-audit of the probability logic: for a fair coin, each flip is independent and stays 50-50 regardless of prior outcomes; a run of heads makes neither heads nor tails more likely next. The expected value in 20 flips is 10 heads, but the actual result varies and clustering near (not exactly at) 10 is normal — all consistent across the source fields.

Correction confirmed: the summary names 'law of small numbers' as the misconception (expecting a small sample to match / inferring bias from too few trials), consistent with the original pedagogy, not as a label for the correct clustering fact.

Correction confirmed: the interpretation-check action asks whether the next flip after a streak is more likely heads, tails, or neither, so 'neither — equally likely' is available; the recency-activity opening action also allows 'cannot be predicted' as a valid response.

Independent re-audit found the probability logic coherent from first action through every feedback item; no further errors or contradictions were introduced, and the two prior corrections hold at every learner-facing occurrence.

The source framing that a linear quiz 'cannot' deliver the conducting skill and dialogue 'cannot' deliver recording practice was softened to scoped affordances/limits rather than universal impossibility claims; the genuine objective limit (recognition-only tasks do not elicit independent construction) is retained.

The claim that a 3D toss 'buys little' over a 2D simulator was reframed as a trade-off (tactile realism vs rapid scaling) rather than a ranking, since comparative efficacy is not established by the sources.

probeDeeper: You got 13 heads and 7 tails — does that prove the coin is unfair? How could you check?
It just landed heads four times in a row. What do you think the next flip will be, and why?
If you flipped it 200 times instead of 20, what would you expect the tally to look like?
Did you get exactly 10 heads? Should you have expected to? Why or why not?
assess.correctAnswer: A correct performance: the child predicts about half (roughly 10 heads), sets up a tally with one row per outcome, marks exactly one tally per flip AS it happens, totals 20 marks for 20 flips, and reads the result sensibly — 'about half, but not exactly ten' — treating it as close to the expected split rather than an exact match, and does not claim the next flip is 'due' to be a particular side.

errorPatterns.pattern: Expects the small experiment to match the theoretical split exactly and concludes the coin is biased when it does not
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do not reteach the mechanics — pool their flips with others' to reach 100+ and show the proportion settling near half; name that 20 trials is too few to judge fairness (the seed of the experimental-vs-theoretical topic)
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On getting 13 heads and 7 tails, declares the coin unfair or that they 'did it wrong'

errorPatterns.pattern: Recency thinking — predicts the next trial from the recent run ('it's been heads four times, tails is due', or 'heads is hot')
errorPatterns.nextMove: State plainly that the coin has no memory — each flip is independent and stays 50-50 regardless of what came before; test it by predicting-then-flipping several times
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Announces a prediction for the next flip based on the previous outcomes, or seems surprised the streak 'kept going'

errorPatterns.pattern: Records carelessly — backfills tallies or loses count so the total does not match the number of trials
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold a one-mark-immediately-per-flip routine and a running count; this is an execution lapse, so support the recording habit rather than reteaching the concept
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Tally total ≠ 20, or the child reconstructs marks from memory after flipping rather than marking each in turn

responseLevels.gap: Records unsystematically (miscounts, backfills) or treats the outcome as predictable/exact; uses recency to predict the next flip; cannot relate the result to the prediction
responseLevels.full: Records systematically one-per-trial, predicts about half, reads the outcome as close-to-but-not-exactly expected, attributes the gap to too few trials, and treats each flip as independent of the last
responseLevels.partial: Records accurately and states an expectation, but reads any deviation as the coin being unfair, expects an exact match, or shows recency thinking — lists results without linking short-run variation to the small number of trials

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child a coin and a blank tally chart and say: 'Before you start, tell me roughly how many heads you expect in 20 flips. Now flip the coin 20 times, recording each result, then tell me what you notice.' (Set the task and WATCH — do not tell them how to record or how to interpret. Watch how they tally, whether they predict the next flip from the last few, and how they explain the gap between 'about 10' and what they actually got.)
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching separates the child who tallies one-mark-per-trial and reads roughly-half sensibly from one who backfills or miscounts, declares the coin broken on getting 13–7, or says 'tails is due' mid-run. The doing exposes law-of-small-numbers and recency beliefs that a written answer would hide.

sources.claim: A small sample need not match the theoretical probability, and concluding bias from too few trials is a documented mistake: '20 times is not enough trials' — the more trials, the closer relative frequency gets to the theoretical probability.

Recency errors — both 'a tail is due' (negative recency, from the representativeness heuristic) and expecting a streak to continue (positive recency) — reflect a failure to treat successive trials as independent, and are documented across childhood.
